# Settings reference

<!-- Generated by band3 --settings_reference (tools/settings_reference.py) from the
     settings registry: don't edit it by hand. A setting's description is in
     src/settings.cpp (or the SDK), its label and section in
     src/Launcher/launcher_settings.cpp. -->

Every setting the launcher and the in-game settings (Escape > Settings) show, category by category, as this build of band3 registers them. Each can be saved in `band3.toml` as `name = value` or passed on the command line as `--name=value`; [Settings, folders and songs](settings.md#config-files) says which wins when several places set one. The defaults are the Windows build's.

## Game

### Folders

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `game_data_root`<br>Game data folder | *(empty)* | text | Override game data path *Applies at the next start.* |
| `content_folders`<br>Song folders | `songs` | text | Folders RB3 reads DLC and custom songs from, without installing them, separated by '\|'. Subfolders count too. A relative folder is relative to band3_config.ini's folder (or band3's own folder if there is no ini) *Applies at the next start.* |
| `user_data_root`<br>User data folder | *(empty)* | text | Override user data path *Applies at the next start.* |

### Profile

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `username`<br>Profile name | *(empty)* | text | Override the username (up to 15 characters): the profile's gamertag wherever the game asks for it, online included. Empty keeps the profile's |
| `lang`<br>Language | *(empty)* | *(empty)* Default, `eng` English, `esl` Spanish, `fre` French, `ita` Italian, `deu` German | Force a language: eng, esl (Spanish), fre, ita or deu. Empty uses the default *Applies at the next start.* |
| `skip_profile_prompt`<br>Guests without a profile | `true` | `true`, `false` | Players who join without a profile join as guests, without the game asking them to choose one (No Profile, Sign In, Swap to User). Off, it asks, as on a console |
| `score_history`<br>Score history | `true` | `true`, `false` | Keep every finished song's results (score, stars, notes hit, streak, overdrive) in score_history.jsonl in the user data folder, for the web page's History tab and its played and stars filters. Songs played on autoplay aren't kept |

### Startup

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `show_launcher`<br>Open the launcher at startup | `true` | `true`, `false` | Show the launcher, band3's setup screen, before the game starts. Off, band3 starts the game straight away; hold Shift as it starts, or start it with --launcher, to see the launcher anyway *Applies at the next start.* |
| `fast_start`<br>Skip the splash screens | `false` | `true`, `false` | Skip the splash screens once the game has finished initializing *Applies at the next start.* |
| `autosave`<br>Autosave | `true` | `true`, `false` | Let the game autosave profiles, after songs and setlist edits. Off, they're only saved from the options menu, e.g. to test with autoplay without touching your profile |
| `disable_metamusic`<br>Menu music | `false` | `true`, `false` | Disable the background menu music *Applies at the next start.* |

## Gameplay

### Speed

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `song_speed`<br>Song speed | `1` | `0.1` to `10` (x) | Plays songs faster or slower: 1.5 is half again as fast, 0.75 three quarters. Applies from the next song. A speed other than 1 that practice mode or Rock Band 3 Deluxe's song speed sets is left as it is |
| `track_speed`<br>Note speed | `1` | `0.1` to `10` (x) | Scrolls the note highway faster or slower: 2 is twice as fast, with the notes twice as far apart. Applies from the next song |

### Unlocks

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unlock_clothing`<br>Unlock all clothing | `false` | `true`, `false` | Unlock every piece of clothing, tattoo and face paint for your characters, and the video venues, without earning them (RB3Enhanced's UnlockClothing) |
| `gold_on_all_difficulties`<br>Gold stars on every difficulty | `false` | `true`, `false` | Let gold stars be earned on every difficulty, not only expert (RB3Enhanced's AllowGoldOnAllDifficulties). Applies from the next song |

### Song list

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `game_origin_icons`<br>Song source icons | `true` | `true`, `false` | Show an icon in the song list for the game or pack each song came from (RB3Enhanced's GameOriginIcons). Needs Rock Band 3 Deluxe's icons and a song list with a game_origin_icon slot. Applies the next time the song list opens |

### Venue

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `forced_venue`<br>Venue | `false` | text; `false` Game's pick, `arena` Arena, `big_club` Big club, `small_club` Small club, `festival` Festival, `video` Video venue, `none` None (black) | Venue to force, applied from the next venue load. false = don't force. A venue (arena_04), a class (arena, big_club, small_club, festival, video), none for a black background, or a comma separated list to pick from at random |

## Display

### Screen

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `monitor`<br>Monitor | `0` | `0` to `16`; `0` Default, `1` Primary, `2` Monitor 2, `3` Monitor 3, `4` Monitor 4 | Monitor index to display on (0 = default, 1 = primary, 2 = second monitor, etc.) |
| `fullscreen`<br>Window mode | `false` | `true`, `false` | Start the window in fullscreen mode |
| `fullscreen_exclusive`<br>Exclusive fullscreen | `false` | `true`, `false` | Switch the display mode in fullscreen instead of going borderless at the desktop mode |
| `resolution`<br>Window size | *(empty)* | text; *(empty)* Default, `720p` 1280 x 720, `1080p` 1920 x 1080, `1440p` 2560 x 1440, `4k` 3840 x 2160 | Common resolution preset for both guest video mode and window (for example: 720p, 1080p, 1440p, 4k, 1280x720) |
| `present_letterbox`<br>Picture shape | `true` | `true`, `false` | Enable letterboxing for non-native aspect ratios |
| `native_fill_window`<br>Fill the window | `true` | `true`, `false` | Native renderer (renderer native or both): draw the game at the window's shape rather than 16:9 with black bars. A wider window (21:9) shows more to the sides, a taller one (16:10) more above and below, with the HUD and tracks at their size in the middle 16:9. The emulated GPU's picture stays 16:9 |
| `steam_deck_defaults`<br>Steam Deck settings | `true` | `true`, `false` | On a Steam Deck, start fullscreen and letterboxed at the console's 60 Hz with vsync on and the FPS counter off, unless band3.toml or the command line set those *Applies at the next start.* |

### Smoothness

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `frame_cap`<br>Frame rate cap | `display` | text; `display` Match the display, `auto` Just under the display, `off` Off (the console's 60), `60` 60 fps, `120` 120 fps, `144` 144 fps, `180` 180 fps, `240` 240 fps | What paces the game's frames. display: the display's refresh rate exactly (119.88 Hz, not 120), for fixed-refresh displays (the default). auto: a little under it (5% less, at least 4 fps), for VRR displays (G-Sync, FreeSync), keeping each frame inside their range; on a fixed-refresh display a cap under the refresh rate shows a frame twice every 1/(refresh - cap) seconds. A number of Hz (24 to 240), e.g. 117. off: the emulated console's vertical blank, paced by vsync and video_mode_refresh_rate (60 unless set). With the cap on, vsync is turned off and an unset video_mode_refresh_rate follows the cap. Without a display whose rate can be told, display and auto are off |
| `native_present_pacing`<br>Smooth frame pacing | `true` | `true`, `false` | With the native picture shown, publish each frame to the window a steady delay after the game presented it (about the slowest recent frame's), so frames that draw quickly (with even/odd rendering, every other one) don't reach a paint together with the one before; off publishes each as soon as it's drawn, to compare. Only while the game runs under 1.5 times the display's refresh rate, frame_cap isn't auto and native_phase_lock isn't steering the cap on a display of 100 Hz or more: faster, each refresh shows the newest frame anyway, auto's variable refresh display shows each as it comes, and there the phase lock already has each frame reach the window before its paint, so the delay would only add lag. Below 100 Hz the lock keeps it, as frames vary more against the refresh |
| `debug_overlay`<br>FPS counter | `true` | `true`, `false` | Show band3's FPS counter: the game's frame rate (what frame_cap paces, and hit timing follows) and the window's, which the display's refresh rate holds back |

## Graphics

### Renderer

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `renderer`<br>Renderer | `native` | `native` Native, `emulated` Emulated, `both` Both (debug) | What draws the picture. native: band3's own renderer alone, no emulated Xbox 360 GPU (the default on Windows, and on a Steam Deck through its presets). emulated: the emulated GPU alone (the default elsewhere). both, Native + emulated (debug): the two, F8 switching between their pictures. Native to or from the others applies at the next start. Band3/Graphics/Native applies to native and both; Band3/Graphics/Emulated and the emulated GPU's own (under GPU, there only in a run with it) to emulated and both |
| `emulated_gpu_while_native`<br>Emulated GPU's work | `skip_draws` | `full` Everything, `skip_draws` Only what's needed, `swap_only` What the game waits on (test) | Renderer both only: what the emulated GPU still does while the native picture shows: skip_draws leaves out the game's draws nobody sees (the native renderer draws them), keeping what RB3 draws once (outfits) so F8 back shows the game's picture; full draws everything, as with the emulated picture shown. swap_only also skips clears, resolves, the flares' occlusion-test quads and the passes RB3 draws once, leaving only what the game waits on: a test and performance mode, after which F8 back to emulated may show black outfits, portraits and other stale pictures until RB3 draws them again |
| `emulated_gpu`<br>Emulated GPU | *(empty)* | *(empty)*, `on`, `off` | Retired: set renderer instead. Read at startup for one more release: off is renderer native, on with renderer native is renderer both, on with renderer emulated stays emulated (a renderer set on the command line, or already both, wins). Then cleared *Applies at the next start.* |

### Quality

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `native_view_msaa`<br>Anti-aliasing | `2` | `1` Off, `2` Game's (2x), `4` 4x | Native renderer (renderer native or both) and the native view (experimental): the samples a pixel they draw the HUD, the track and the menus over the world with, averaged at their edges: 2 = the game's (RB3 multisamples them, not the world), 4 smoother, 1 none |
| `swap_post_effect`<br>Anti-aliasing | `none` | `none` Off, `fxaa` FXAA, `fxaa_extreme` FXAA (extreme) | Swap post effect: none, fxaa, fxaa_extreme *Applies at the next start.* |
| `native_anisotropic`<br>Texture filtering | `-1` | `-1` Default, `0` Off, `1` 1x, `2` 2x, `3` 4x, `4` 8x, `5` 16x | Native renderer (renderer native or both): the anisotropic filtering it samples textures with, as the emulated GPU's anisotropic_override counts it: 0 off, 1 = 1x, 2 = 2x, 3 = 4x, 4 = 8x, 5 = 16x. -1 (the default) follows anisotropic_override where the emulated GPU runs (both), so the two pictures match, and keeps the game's own otherwise |
| `anisotropic_override`<br>Texture filtering | `3` | `-1` Default, `0` Off, `1` 1x, `2` 2x, `3` 4x, `4` 8x, `5` 16x | Forces anisotropic filtering for eligible textures. Higher values keep textures sharper at oblique angles, but increase texture sampling cost.  -1 = No override   0 = Disable anisotropic filtering   1 = Force 1x anisotropic filtering   2 = Force 2x anisotropic filtering   3 = Force 4x anisotropic filtering   4 = Force 8x anisotropic filtering   5 = Force 16x anisotropic filtering |
| `native_max_height`<br>Render size cap | `0` | `0` to `4320`; `0` Window's size, `360` 360p, `480` 480p, `540` 540p, `720` 720p, `1080` 1080p, `1440` 1440p, `2160` 4K | Native renderer (renderer native or both): the most lines it draws: a window taller than this has its picture drawn this tall and scaled up to fill it, for 4K on a GPU that can't draw it at full size. 0 = the window's size |
| `native_view_shadow_scale`<br>Shadows | `1` | `1` Game's (512), `2` High (1024), `3` Higher (1536), `4` Highest (2048) | Draw the characters' self-shadow maps this many times the game's 512x512 in the native renderer and the native view (experimental): sharper shadow edges. 1 = the game's |
| `resolution_scale`<br>Render scale | `1` | `1` to `8` (x) | Draw resolution scale for both X and Y axes (same as setting draw_resolution_scale_x and draw_resolution_scale_y) *Applies at the next start.* |

### Effects

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `disable_hair_shader`<br>Hair shader | `false` | `true`, `false` | Don't use the hair shader variation on materials. Applies to materials loaded afterwards |
| `disable_approximate_lights`<br>Approximate lighting | `true` | `true`, `false` | Disable approximate lighting; works around a graphical bug in current ReXGlue |
| `force_self_shadow`<br>Self-shadows in every shot | `false` | `true`, `false` | Draw the band's self-shadows in every camera shot, also the ones that turn them off. Characters far from the camera and the crowd still draw without them. Some of those shots may show shadow artifacts the game avoided there. Applies from the next shot |
| `compress_character_textures`<br>Compress character textures | `false` | `true`, `false` | Compress character textures. Needs the emulated GPU (renderer emulated or both): it's ignored with renderer native, where nothing composes the outfits to read back and they'd show black. Needs readback resolve, or the textures appear bugged. Applies to characters loaded afterwards |

### Timing

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rnd_sync`<br>Game frame sync | `1` | `-1` Game's pick, `0` Off, `1` On | Vertical sync: -1 = don't override, 0 = off, 1 = on *Applies at the next start.* |
| `background_fps`<br>Venue frame rate | `0` | `0` to `240` (fps); `0` Venue's own | The venue's frame rate under even/odd rendering: 0 = the venue's own (30 in most), whatever the game's refresh rate, or that many fps (at most the refresh rate). RB3 counts it as if the game ran at 60, so at a video_mode_refresh_rate of 120 a venue's 30 drew at 60 |
| `vsync`<br>VSync | `true` | `true`, `false` | Enable vertical sync |

### Performance

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `native_post_effects`<br>Bloom, depth of field, motion blur | `true` | `true`, `false` | Native renderer (renderer native or both): the camera's post-processing effects, bloom (and glare), depth of field and motion blur. Off leaves them out for a slower GPU; the venue's colours, the spotlights' haze, soft particles and film grain stay. On a Radeon 680M at 1920x1200 in arena_04 that's 1.5 ms less GPU work a post frame (busy 11.8 to 10.7 ms). Applies from the next frame |
| `native_world_ahead_auto`<br>Draw ahead on integrated GPUs | `true` | `true`, `false` | Draw the world ahead (native_world_ahead) by itself on an integrated GPU (one that shares the system's memory, as a laptop's does) and on a Steam Deck: on a Radeon 680M at 1920x1200, 60 Hz, a song's post frames went from 11.1 to 6.2 ms, latency from 22.5 to 17.5 ms and repeated frames fell by a sixth, the picture the same. Not on other GPUs: a fast desktop one at 120 Hz did worse with it. native_world_ahead on draws it ahead on any GPU either way; with this off, only that does. On Linux neither does while native_upload_pipeline is on, its default. The log says which applied, with the GPU's name *Windows only.* |
| `native_world_ahead`<br>Draw ahead on every GPU | `false` | `true`, `false` | Experimental: with RB3's even/odd rendering, draw each world frame's venue on the GPU right after that frame, without waiting for it, so the post frame after it only post-processes it and draws the track and HUD. The world's GPU time moves into the world frame's half of the pair: on a 60 Hz laptop post frames went from 14 to 8 ms and the picture's latency fell 3 to 6 ms, the picture the same. Where post frames drawn this way still run about a frame's time it skips more frames than without, so it measures both every few seconds and keeps the one that skips fewer. On draws it ahead on any GPU; off leaves it to native_world_ahead_auto, which does on an integrated GPU or a Steam Deck (a laptop's Radeon 680M at 60 Hz: 5 ms less latency, a sixth fewer repeated frames) and not on other GPUs, as on a fast desktop GPU at 120 Hz it made things worse. It sends GPU work it doesn't wait for, as the setup that once hung AMD GPUs did (not seen with this one). Not with native_present_pipeline on, or on Linux native_upload_pipeline (on by default), which wait differently *Windows only.* |
| `native_deferred_decode_threads`<br>Texture decode threads | `2` | `0` to `3`; `0` Off | How many threads help the native renderer decode the textures and meshes a song's first frames and a camera cut show for the first time (over 4 MB of them), so it holds the last frame for less time; they sleep the rest of the time. 0 decodes them on the renderer's own thread, as before. The picture is the same either way |

### Microphones

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `usb_mics`<br>PC microphones | `false` | `true`, `false` | Experimental: sing through microphones on this PC, as Xbox 360 USB microphones *Applies at the next start.* |
| `usb_mic_devices`<br>Microphones | *(empty)* | text | Microphones to sing through, or part of their names, comma separated, one per mic slot (up to 3). Empty uses the system's default recording device *Applies at the next start.* |

The game's gentle pitch correction (Solo vocals) isn't heard |

### Instruments

|---|---|---|---|
| `controller_type`<br>Gamepads play as | `7` | `-1` Game's pick, `1` Vocals, `7` Guitar, `8` Drums | Instrument gamepads and the keyboard play as: -1 = don't override, 1 = vocals, 7 = guitar, 8 = drums. Instruments that report their own type (Xbox 360 instruments with input_backend = xinput, the virtual instrument) keep it *Applies at the next start.* |
| `guitar_type`<br>Guitars play as | `auto` | `auto` Auto, `rock_band` Rock Band guitars, `guitar_hero` Guitar Hero guitars | What RB3 takes guitars for: auto = what each reports itself, rock_band = Rock Band guitars, whose pickup switch picks the overdrive effect, guitar_hero = Guitar Hero guitars, which have no effect switch. A Guitar Hero guitar played as a Rock Band one changes the effect when it's turned face up. auto can't tell on Linux, or for a guitar that isn't an Xbox 360 one; choose guitar_hero for a Guitar Hero guitar there *Applies at the next start.* |
| `hid_instruments`<br>Other consoles' instruments | `false` | `true`, `false` | Experimental: play PS3, Wii, PS4 and PS5 Rock Band guitars and drum kits (and the MIDI Pro Adapter in drum mode) through their USB dongles, and on Windows Xbox One ones through GameInput 3, as Xbox 360 instruments *Applies at the next start.* |
| `input_backend`<br>Controller reading | `sdl` | `sdl` SDL, `xinput` XInput | Input backend: sdl, xinput *Applies at the next start.* *Windows only.* |

### Drums

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `midi_drums`<br>MIDI drum kit | `false` | `true`, `false` | Play a MIDI drum kit as a Rock Band pro drum kit, without a MIDI Pro Adapter *Applies at the next start.* |

## Music Videos

### Playback

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `music_videos`<br>Music videos | `true` | `true`, `false` | Play a song's music video in the video venues, in place of their background clips, when music_videos_folder has one for it: &lt;shortname&gt;.mp4 (or .mkv, .mov, .webm...), and optionally &lt;shortname&gt;.ini with Clone Hero's video_start_time. forced_venue video picks the video venues. Turned on, it applies from the next song |
| `music_video_venue_chance`<br>Video venue | `100` | `0` Never, `25` A quarter of the time, `50` Half the time, `75` Most of the time, `100` Always | How often a song with a music video is put in a video venue, so its video shows, in percent: 0 never (the game's venue), 25, 50, 75 or 100 always. A forced venue and the black background modifier still win. Applies from the next venue the game picks |
| `music_video_hide_band`<br>Hide the band | `true` | `true`, `false` | Leave the band out of the picture while a song's music video plays, so only the video shows behind the highways. The venue's lights (and Stage Kit) go on as before |
| `music_video_as_is`<br>Without the venue's filters | `true` | `true`, `false` | Show a song's music video as it is: the video venue's colour filter, film grain, glow and trails are left off while it plays (and on the black background's black) |
| `music_video_full_rate`<br>Smooth 60 fps videos | `true` | `true`, `false` | Play a music video faster than the venue's 30 fps (a 60 fps one) at its own frame rate: the video venue is drawn that fast while it plays (as background_fps would, up to the game's rate), which takes about twice the drawing and decoding. Off, it shows at the venue's rate |
| `music_video_auto_sync`<br>Sync videos by themselves | `true` | `true`, `false` | Find each music video's offset from its sound: when its song is picked, the song's audio (read from its package or the game's archive, decrypted if need be, or for a song band3 can't read taken as it first plays, about 45 s in) is matched against the video's and a sure match is saved as video_start_time in the video's .ini, and used at once. An .ini that sets one is left alone |
| `music_videos_folder`<br>Videos folder | `videos` | text | The folder music videos are looked for in (empty: videos). A relative folder is relative to band3_config.ini's folder (or band3's own folder if there is no ini) |
| `music_video_fit`<br>Video shape | `fit` | `fit` Letterbox, `fill` Crop to fill, `stretch` Stretch | How a music video whose shape isn't the screen's is shown: fit (all of it, with black bars), fill (the whole screen, its edges cut off) or stretch |

### Finding videos

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `music_video_ytdlp_path`<br>yt-dlp program | *(empty)* | text | yt-dlp, which finds and downloads songs' music videos from the Music Videos screen: its program file (yt-dlp.exe). Empty looks for yt-dlp on PATH. band3 doesn't come with it: get it from github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp |

| `music_video_prefer_60fps`<br>Download 60 fps videos | `true` | `true`, `false` | Download a music video's 60 fps picture where it has one (music_video_full_rate plays it at 60); off, its 30 fps one |
| `music_video_auto_accept`<br>Accept clear matches | `true` | `true`, `false` | When finding music videos, take one without asking when it's surely the song's: its title, channel and length look right and its sound matches the song's. Off, every song's results wait on the Music Videos screen for you to choose |
| `music_video_keep_audio`<br>Keep the videos' sound | `false` | `true`, `false` | Keep a downloaded music video's sound (in the videos folder's .sync folder), so it can be aligned again with its song; band3 plays the video under the game's own sound, so it's otherwise deleted once the video is synced |

## Advanced

### Game code

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `audio_idle_bypass` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Skip the game's audio effects while all they do is process silence: the microphones' pitch correction, EQ, compressor and echo while no microphone is connected, and the reverb and the other effects while nothing reaches them. Each is skipped once what it plays has stayed below -144 dB for 5 seconds (a compressor's gain must have stopped moving too: the microphones' takes about 20 seconds), runs again on the first sound that reaches it, and none is skipped while a microphone is connected. On a Ryzen 6850U laptop it saves about 1.5-1.8 ms of the audio thread's CPU a frame in a song (of 2.6-2.8) and 2 ms paused (of 2.4). Off runs every effect all the time, as the game does on a console |
| `audio_xapo_nonblocking` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Answer the game's checks of whether each sound effect is still playing (dozens a frame, through its voice's effect parameters) with the newest result the audio thread set, instead of waiting for the audio thread's next pass to reach a sound that's starting or fading out: up to about 10 ms here, more than a frame at 120 Hz. Off waits, as the game does on a console (up to 5 ms there) |
| `fast_heap_search` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Linux: find where the game's memory allocations go in the guest heap by skipping each allocated region whole, rather than one page at a time as the SDK does, then let the SDK allocate there: the same place, found faster. The game's physical allocations search 512 MB of 4 KB pages mostly full near the top; on a Steam Deck that was about 40 ms of the game thread in 28 s of a song, in bursts (0.4 ms of the frame a song starts in) |
| `fast_heap_search_check` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Linux, with fast_heap_search: run the SDK's own search for each allocation instead, and log any place it chose that fast_heap_search wouldn't have (none should). For checking fast_heap_search |
| `native_camera_shake` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Use the frame-rate independent camera shake replacement *Applies at the next start.* |
| `native_math` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Use native C++ replacements for the game's math functions (sin, cos, pow, vector/matrix ops) |
| `native_vorbis` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Run two parts of the game's Vorbis decoder as native code: the inverse MDCT, which turns each block of a song's audio into samples and is about a third of the decoding, and the codebook decoding, which reads the packed values each block is made from and is about a quarter. Both compute exactly what the game's own do, every sample the same. On a Ryzen 6850U laptop the inverse MDCT saves about 0.35 ms of the decode thread's CPU a frame in a song (of 1.3) and the codebook decoding about 0.25 ms more (1.0 to 0.75). Off runs the game's own |
| `native_vorbis_check` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Run both the game's and native_vorbis's inverse MDCT and codebook decoding on every block of the songs' audio, play the game's, and log every 5 seconds how many samples and decoded values came out different and by how much (none should). For checking native_vorbis; it costs more CPU than either |
| `preload_song_start_resources` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Keep ui/resource/fonts/instruments_icons_rings.milo loaded for the whole session, as the game keeps its other fonts from boot. Otherwise the game reads it again as each song starts, in that song's slowest frame (2.3 ms of the game's thread on a Steam Deck), which could then miss its paint. Costs one small font's memory |
| `vr_show_all` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Experimental, for VR: draw the whole world in every camera shot, ignoring what each shot hides and what lies outside the game's camera |

| `game_stall_log_ms` | `100` | `0` to `100000` | Log each of the game's frames that takes longer than this many milliseconds, with samples of the game thread's stack and what else was going on (src/stall_watch.h); at most one every two seconds. 0 = off |
| `log_net_calls` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Log each of the game's network calls (sockets, XNet) and what it returned |

### Native renderer

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `native_bc_textures` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Keep RB3's compressed textures (DXT1, DXT3, DXT5, DXN) compressed on the GPU, as BC1, BC2, BC3 and BC5, where it has those formats: the native renderer decodes a song's or a shot's new textures in a fraction of the time, and they take a quarter to an eighth of the video memory, upload and bandwidth. The picture differs only by the GPU's decoder rounding a colour by a step or two. Off decodes them to RGBA as before, to compare; applies to textures seen after the change |
| `native_gpu_draw_profile` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With native_gpu_timestamps, also time each world draw on the GPU (a timestamp before every one) and log every 10 seconds the meshes and materials that took the most, for finding what makes the world slow. Its timestamps cost GPU time of their own, so it's off unless profiling |
| `native_gpu_timestamps` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Time each native renderer frame's parts on the GPU (the world, its texture passes, post-processing, the overlay...) with GPU timestamps, for the slow-frame log and the test harness's numbers. Direct3D 12 and Vulkan. On costs a few dozen timestamps a frame, 0.1 to 0.2 ms of the frame's wait for the GPU, so it's off unless measuring |
| `native_keep_carried_passes` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Keep what the native renderer drew for a texture the game drew in an earlier frame and hasn't drawn since (the characters' outfits, skin and hair, carried into each frame's capture), rather than drawing it again every frame: it's drawn again when the game draws it again, or a setting that changes how it's drawn does. The picture is the same; at 1080p on a Steam Deck the texture passes took about 4 ms of the GPU a frame. Off draws them every frame, as before, to compare |
| `native_phase_lock` | `true` | `true`, `false` | With the native picture shown and the frame cap at a fixed rate (display or a number matching the display's), move the cap's beat so each frame reaches the window a set time (native_phase_lock_slack) before the paint that shows it, rather than wherever the cap's clock happens to fall against the display's: a frame a little slower than the rest then still makes its paint instead of being shown a refresh late and the next skipped |
| `native_phase_lock_slack` | `0` | `0` to `90` | With native_phase_lock, how long before the paint that shows it the median frame should reach the window, in percent of a refresh: less is less lag, until frames a little slower than the rest miss their paint. 0, the default, picks by the display's rate: 65 at 100 Hz or more (at 120 Hz post-processed frames run about 1.9 ms behind the median, and 65 repeated 83% fewer frames than 50 for 1.2 ms more lag), 50 below, where 50 is already 8.3 ms at 60 Hz. 10 to 90 sets it |
| `native_present_pipeline` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With the native picture shown, on the zero-copy path, record the next frame while the GPU draws the one before, waiting for the GPU only to hand a frame to the window, so a frame costs the longer of its CPU and GPU time rather than both (for 120 Hz); off waits for each frame right after sending it. Keep it off: it hangs AMD GPUs and grows video memory steadily (about 10 MB a second at 120 Hz: the SDL_gpu allocations it makes aren't released on this path) |
| `native_present_request_paint` | `true` | `true`, `false` | With renderer native (no emulated GPU), ask the window to paint each time the native renderer has a new frame for it, as the emulated GPU's swaps did; off leaves the window to paint when something else asks, to compare |
| `native_present_trace` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With the native picture shown, log each frame the native renderer hands the window (its Present, the worker taking it, its submission, finish and publishing, in steady-clock ns, and its record and GPU wait ms) and each paint (its time, and the frame it shows), to tell why a frame was shown twice or skipped. Kept in memory and logged when the harness's present_stats reads the stretch (a reset drops them), so logging doesn't hold up the frames; about 120 lines a second |
| `native_present_zero_copy` | `true` | `true`, `false` | With the native picture shown (renderer native or both), show the GPU's frames where they are, on the GPU (Direct3D 12, when band3's renderer shares the game's device); off reads each frame back and uploads it, the way other platforms do, to compare |
| `native_query_log` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Log what the occlusion queries (the lens flares' visibility tests) give the game: the result of its first 50 reads of a query, then one a second at most, with either GPU; with renderer native also the counts the first 20 query packets found. Turning it on again logs as many more |
| `native_query_sample_count` | `-1` | `-1` to `1000000` | What the occlusion queries (the lens flares' visibility tests) report as drawn. -1, the default: the pixels each test covers on screen, as a 360 reports with nothing in front of the flare, so flares draw at their full strength, with either GPU (nothing hides them: what's in front isn't tested). 0 or more: every query reports that many with renderer native, and the emulated GPU its own query_occlusion_fake_sample_count (1000, what RB3 got before, which left a large flare at a few percent of its strength) |
| `native_r8_textures` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Keep RB3's one-channel textures (k_8: the planes of its movies, the intro, the menus' backgrounds and the music-video venues' screens, new each frame of a movie) a byte a texel on the GPU, as R8, where it has that format, rather than four: a quarter of the video memory, upload and decoding. The picture is the same. Off sends them as RGBA as before, to compare; applies to textures seen after the change |
| `native_slow_frame_ms` | `12` | `0` to `10000` | With the native picture shown, log a line for each frame the native renderer takes longer than this many milliseconds to draw (its GPU wait included), with what kind of frame it was, where the time went and what it had to send or make; at most a few a second. 0 = off |
| `native_sync_short_wait_us` | `0` | `0` to `16000` | With renderer native (no emulated GPU), how the GPU's command processor waits between polls of a wait whose interval is short (under 0x100): 0 yields and polls again at once, as the emulated GPU does; more sleeps that many microseconds instead |
| `native_upload_pipeline` | `true` | `true`, `false` | With the native picture shown, on the upload path (Vulkan, where the window can't sample the native renderer's frames in place), record the next frame while the GPU draws and reads back the one before, so a frame costs the longer of its CPU and GPU time rather than both; off waits for each frame and its read-back right after sending it |
| `native_vblank_free_running` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With renderer native (no emulated GPU), raise the vertical blank every millisecond whatever the frame cap says, as the emulated GPU's vsync off does: with frame_cap off and rnd_sync 0 too, nothing paces the game (uncapped, to measure). Off, it runs at the game's refresh rate unless the frame cap paces the game |
| `native_view_backend` | `gpu` | `cpu`, `gpu` | What draws the native view (F9, experimental) and the native renderer: gpu, or cpu for the reference rasterizer. The GPU falls back to the CPU when it can't start |
| `native_view_capture_profile` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Time each step of the native view's capture on the game's thread (geometry, textures, shade states, bones...) for the test harness's native_view stats, at a clock read per step; its hooks' totals are timed either way |
| `native_view_hardware_sampling` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Let the GPU's own texture samplers filter the textures that fill their texture array layer, in place of the shader filtering them as the game's samplers do: the same filters, mip levels, wrapping and anisotropy, rounded as the GPU rounds them, for much less GPU time. Textures the device's samplers can't do (padded into a larger layer, mirrored once, a border) keep the shader's. Off filters every texture in the shader, as before |
| `native_view_hoist_passes` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Draw the pictures RB3 draws into one texture again and again in a frame (the crowd's, one per kind of character) each into a layer of its own, ahead of the world, so the world draws in one go: the same picture for less CPU time. Off draws them where the game does, to compare |
| `native_view_inline_mips` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Make the mips of the textures RB3 draws into (the crowd's, in a song, several times a frame) in the native renderer's own command buffers, exactly as SDL's mipmap generation makes them, rather than in one more command buffer each: half the command buffers a frame and a little less of the GPU waiting for the CPU. Direct3D 12 only. Off has SDL make them, as before, to compare |
| `native_view_instancing` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Draw runs of the same mesh that differ only in where each one stands (the crowd's cards) as one instanced draw: the same picture for much less CPU time. Off draws each by itself, to compare |
| `native_view_mip_submits` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Hand the GPU a frame's work after each texture pass with mips (the crowd's, several times a frame in a song), so it draws them while the worker records the rest. Off keeps them in the frame's command buffer: post frames wait about 0.35 ms more for the GPU, but with AMD's Direct3D 12 driver a frame's 9 or 10 command buffers had it remap command memory now and then (6.5 ms a time in a VM), which off avoids. With native_view_inline_mips only; the picture is the same |
| `native_view_normal_maps` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Shade RB3's normal maps and detail maps in the native view (experimental), live and in the test harness's captures; off shades those materials with the vertex normal, to compare |
| `native_view_premake_arrays` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Make the GPU texture arrays the textures RB3 loads will go in as it loads them, a few between frames, rather than in the frame that first draws them: a song's first frame made 19 (about 12 ms). The picture is the same; off makes them as before, to compare |
| `native_view_premake_targets` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Make the textures RB3 draws into (outfits, faces, the crowd) as it loads them, a few between frames, rather than in the frame that first draws them: a song's first camera cut to the band made 25 of them in one frame (about 25 ms). Those without depth share one depth texture per size. The picture is the same; off makes them as before, to compare |
| `native_view_record_targets` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Record the passes RB3 draws into textures (outfits, the crowd, blurs) all the time, for the native view (experimental), even while it's off: some are drawn once, in the main menu, and a later capture needs them. Costs a little game-thread time while characters load; turn it on at launch (--native_view_record_targets=true) |
| `native_view_render_scale` | `1` | `0.25` to `4` | For measuring: the native renderer draws its picture at this times the window's size (after native_max_height), its screen-sized passes with it, and the window shows it scaled to fit, to see what the GPU does at a size the window can't reach (VR's eyes). 1 = the window's size |
| `native_view_rt_fallback` | `guest` | `guest`, `none` | What the native view's capture keeps of a texture RB3 draws at runtime (outfits, the crowd, blurs): guest also decodes what guest memory holds, right only with --readback_resolve=full; none keeps only which texture and version it is, for the texture passes the capture records |
| `native_view_shader_variants` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Draw the common venue materials with smaller versions of the mesh shader, each with the features those materials don't use left out: the same picture for less GPU time. Off draws every material with the one shader that does them all |
| `native_view_submit_points` | `1` | `0` to `1` | Where the native renderer hands a frame to the GPU in parts, so the GPU draws the first while the worker records the rest: 0 = only after each texture pass with mips (the crowd's, in a song); 1 = also once the world is recorded, so the GPU draws it while the worker records post-processing and the HUD (in a song its post frames waited about 0.3 ms less for the GPU; the picture is the same) |
| `native_view_target_scale` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Draw the native renderer's passes that are pictures of the screen (the spotlights' haze, the soft particles' smoke) in proportion to its picture: 1.5 times the game's size at 1080p, 3 times at 4K. Off keeps the game's sizes, made for 1280x720, to compare |
| `native_view_texture_filtering` | `true` | `true`, `false` | Sample textures in the native view (experimental) as the game's samplers do: filtered, between mip levels by distance, and clamped or wrapped as each says, live and in the test harness's captures; off reads every texture's nearest texel at full size, to compare |
| `vr` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Experimental: show the native renderer's picture in a VR headset through OpenXR (Windows), each eye drawn from where it is in the venue, the track, the HUD and the menus on a panel in front of you (vr_hud). Needs the native renderer and an OpenXR runtime, such as SteamVR, which starting it opens; the window shows the left eye *Applies at the next start.* |
| `vr_anchor` | `0,-1250,520,0` | text | With vr: where the headset's starting point is in the venue, as x,y,z in inches (x right, y towards the stage, z up) and a turn in degrees, counterclockwise seen from above (0 faces the stage); the default is above and behind the crowd in front of the stage. Empty follows the game's camera, facing where it looks |
| `vr_fake_pose` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With vr: turn the head slowly from side to side instead of where the headset says it is, to test without one (SteamVR's null driver doesn't move) |
| `vr_hud` | `true` | `true`, `false` | With vr: show the track, the HUD and the menus on a flat panel in front of you, as the game draws them. Off shows the venue alone. Takes effect at once |
| `vr_hud_below` | `0.25` | `-5` to `5` | With vr_hud: how far below your eyes the panel's centre is, in metres (negative raises it); the panel tilts back to face you. Takes effect at once |
| `vr_hud_distance` | `1.8` | `0.3` to `20` | With vr_hud: how far ahead of you the panel hangs, in metres, from where you faced at the last recenter. Takes effect at once |
| `vr_hud_recenter` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With vr_hud: a button: each change of this setting (either way) moves the panel back in front of where you face now. The panel is also placed where you first faced, and again when the headset's own recenter moves its seated position |
| `vr_hud_width` | `55` | `10` to `160` | With vr_hud: how wide the panel looks, in degrees across from where you are; its height follows at 16:9. Takes effect at once |
| `vr_world_scale` | `1` | `0.1` to `100` | With vr: how much smaller the venue looks than life size, so a head's movement goes this many times as far in it. 1 = life size |

### Scrobbling

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lastfm_api_url` | `https://ws.audioscrobbler.com/2.0/` | text | Last.fm's API address, which scrobbling calls (lastfm_enabled) *Applies at the next start.* |
| `listenbrainz_api_url` | `https://api.listenbrainz.org` | text | ListenBrainz's API address, which scrobbling calls (listenbrainz_enabled) *Applies at the next start.* |

### Startup

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `launcher` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Show the launcher at this start whatever show_launcher says. Meant for the command line (--launcher), e.g. in Steam's launch options, or the environment; a value in band3.toml is ignored, and it's cleared once read, so "Save to config" can't keep it *Read as band3 starts.* |
| `relaunch_wait_pid` | `0` | a whole number | Set by band3 when it relaunches itself (rb3e_relaunch_game): the new one waits for this process to close before starting. Cleared once it has *Read as band3 starts.* |
| `settings_reference` | *(empty)* | text | Write the settings reference (docs/settings-reference.md: every setting, its default, values and description, from this build) to this file and quit without starting the game. tools/settings_reference.py runs it *Read as band3 starts.* |

### Test harness

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `autoplay` | `false` | `true`, `false` | The game plays every part itself, from the next song start: for repeatable profiling runs and for checking a song without playing it |
| `liveless_gateway` | *(empty)* | text | Where liveless_port_mapping sends PCP and NAT-PMP (host[:port], port 5351 by default) instead of the router, for testing against a stand-in. Empty asks the default gateway; under the test harness, empty skips PCP and NAT-PMP *Applies at the next start.* |
| `liveless_upnp_url` | *(empty)* | text | The UPnP router description liveless_port_mapping uses (http://host:port/desc.xml) instead of looking for one on the network, for testing against a stand-in. Under the test harness, empty skips UPnP *Applies at the next start.* |
| `music_video_test_pattern` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Draw a test pattern in place of the video venues' movie frames (their backgrounds): a white border, a grey ramp, a moving bar and four colour quadrants |
| `stagekit_fake` | `false` | `true`, `false` | With stagekit_usb on: add a pretend USB Stage Kit that keeps the commands it's sent, for the harness's lights command |
| `test_port` | `0` | `0` to `65535` | Take test harness commands on this local TCP port (0 = off), for tools/band3ctl.py. Connects the virtual instrument as player 1 *Applies at the next start.* |
| `test_random_seed` | `0` | `0` to `2147483647` | Seed the game's random numbers with this instead of the clock (0 = off), so a fresh profile gets the same band on every launch, for render checks *Applies at the next start.* |
| `test_score_history` | *(empty)* | text | With test_port set: keep score history in this file, autoplay runs included, in place of score_history.jsonl, which a harness session never writes to (empty = keep none) *Applies at the next start.* |
| `usb_mic_test_tone` | `0` | `0` to `2000` | Sing a steady tone at this pitch in Hz into the first mic slot instead of using microphones, to check that the game hears it. 0 = off *Applies at the next start.* |
| `virtual_instrument` | `false` | `true`, `false` | Connect a virtual Xbox 360 instrument, played from the Instrument Lab (F6) |
| `virtual_instrument_player` | `2` | `1` to `4` | Player slot the virtual instrument connects as, 1-4. Other controllers keep their order around it |
| `virtual_instrument_type` | `guitar` | `guitar`, `drums`, `keys`, `pro_guitar_mustang`, `pro_guitar_squier` | Which instrument the virtual instrument is: guitar, drums, keys, pro_guitar_mustang or pro_guitar_squier. Changing it unplugs the instrument for a moment |

## More of the SDK's settings

The SDK's settings band3_config.ini sets that the launcher's and the in-game settings' categories don't show. The in-game settings' **Every SDK setting** (Advanced) lists these with the rest of the SDK's.

| Setting | Default | Takes | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cache_root` | *(empty)* | text | Override shader cache path *Applies at the next start.* |
| `video_mode_refresh_rate` | `60` | `24` to `240` | Guest video mode refresh rate in Hz *Applies at the next start.* |
| `window_width` | `1280` | `0` to `8192` | Window width in logical pixels (0 = use app default) |
| `window_height` | `720` | `0` to `8192` | Window height in logical pixels (0 = use app default) |
| `log_level` | `info` | `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `critical`, `off` | Global log level: trace, debug, info, warn, error, critical, off |

## band3_config.ini

band3 still reads a `band3_config.ini` from the folder it starts in, or the one beside it, as it did before `band3.toml`. Each key sets the setting beside it, but only where nothing else did, and an empty value leaves the setting alone.
